choices: A simile uses 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor does not
A metaphor uses 'like' or 'as'; a simile does not
A simile always exaggerates; a metaphor never does
questions.explain: Both compare things, but only a simile uses 'like' or 'as'.
questions.tip: Simile is similar, with like or as; metaphor just says it is.

questions.q: 'Time is a thief' is an example of...
questions.explain: It says time is a thief, without 'like' or 'as', so it is a metaphor.
questions.tip: No like or as? It is a metaphor.

questions.q: The weather will ___ our plans.
questions.explain: Affect is usually a verb meaning to influence. Effect is usually a noun meaning a result.
questions.tip: Affect is the Action (verb), Effect is the End result (noun).

questions.q: I would rather walk ___ drive.
questions.explain: Than is used for comparisons. Then is about time or order.
questions.tip: ThAn compAres; thEn tells whEn.

questions.q: Don't ___ your keys.
questions.explain: Lose means to misplace. Loose means not tight.
questions.tip: Lose lost an o.

questions.q: My shoelace is ___.
questions.explain: Loose (rhymes with goose) means not tight.
questions.tip: Loose is as loose as a goose.

questions.q: I ___ your apology.
questions.explain: Accept means to receive or agree to.
questions.tip: Accept means Agree to take; Except means Exclude.

questions.q: Everyone came ___ Tom.
questions.explain: Except means 'but not' or 'other than'.
questions.tip: Except and exclude both start with ex.

questions.q: Honesty is an important ___.
questions.explain: A principle is a rule or belief. A principal is the head of a school, or main.
questions.tip: A principle is a ruLE; the principal is your PAL.

questions.q: She wrote the letter on fancy ___.
questions.explain: Stationery (with an e, like envelope) is writing paper. Stationary means not moving.
questions.tip: StationEry with an E is for Envelopes; stationAry with an A means it stAys put.

questions.q: The runner ___ the finish line.
questions.explain: Passed is the past tense of the verb pass. Past is a noun, adjective, or preposition.
questions.tip: Passed is something you did; past is time behind you.

questions.q: He gave me a kind ___ on my drawing.
questions.explain: A compliment is praise. A complement completes or goes well with something.
questions.tip: A complIment is praise, and I like compliments.

questions.q: The root 'bio' (as in biology) means...
questions.explain: Bio comes from Greek for life. Biology is the study of life.
questions.tip: A biography is the story of someone's life.

questions.q: The root 'graph' (as in autograph) means...
questions.explain: Graph comes from Greek for write. An autograph is your own signature.
questions.tip: A paragraph is writing, and a graph is a drawing.

questions.q: The root 'tele' (as in telephone) means...
questions.explain: Tele is Greek for far. A telephone carries sound far away.
questions.tip: A television lets you see things far away.

questions.q: The root 'port' (as in transport) means...
questions.explain: Port comes from Latin portare, to carry.
questions.tip: A porter carries your bags, and transport carries you.

questions.q: The root 'aqua' (as in aquarium) means...
questions.explain: Aqua is Latin for water.
questions.tip: Aquarium, aqua blue: think water!

questions.q: The root 'spect' (as in inspect) means...
questions.explain: Spect comes from Latin for look. Spectators watch.
questions.tip: Spectacles help you see, and spectators watch.

questions.q: The root 'dict' (as in dictate) means...
questions.explain: Dict comes from Latin for say. A dictionary tells what words say.
questions.tip: A dictionary is full of words you can say.

questions.q: The root 'geo' (as in geography) means...
questions.explain: Geo is Greek for earth.
questions.tip: Geography is drawing maps of the earth.

questions.q: The root 'phon' (as in phonics) means...
questions.explain: Phon is Greek for sound, as in telephone and microphone.
questions.tip: Headphones bring sound to your ears.

questions.q: The root 'chron' means time. Which word uses it?
questions.explain: Chronology is the order in which events happen in time.
questions.tip: A chronicle records events in time order.

questions.q: The protagonist of a story is...
questions.explain: The protagonist is the central character the story follows.
questions.tip: The PROtagonist is the PRO, the star player.

questions.q: The antagonist of a story is...
choices: a character or force that opposes the main character
questions.explain: The antagonist creates conflict for the protagonist.
questions.tip: The ANTagonist is ANTI the hero.

questions.q: The setting of a story is...
choices: the time and place it happens
questions.explain: Setting tells when and where a story takes place.
questions.tip: The setting is where and when you set up camp.

questions.q: The climax of a story is...
choices: the turning point or moment of greatest tension
questions.explain: The climax is the high point of the conflict, after the rising action.
questions.tip: The climax is the climb to the top of the story mountain.

questions.q: The theme of a story is...
choices: its central message or lesson about life
questions.explain: Theme is the big idea the author wants readers to understand.
questions.tip: The theme is the lesson you take home with you.

questions.q: A story told in first-person point of view uses...
questions.explain: In first person, the narrator is a character telling the story as 'I'.
questions.tip: First person: I am telling my own story.

questions.q: Foreshadowing is...
choices: hints about what will happen later
questions.explain: Foreshadowing gives clues to future events in a story.
questions.tip: Foreshadowing: the shadow of what is coming falls on the story early.

questions.q: A flashback is...
choices: a scene that shows events from the past
questions.explain: A flashback interrupts the story to show something that happened earlier.
questions.tip: A flashback flashes BACK in time.

questions.q: The resolution of a story is...
choices: the part where the conflict is resolved
questions.explain: The resolution comes at the end and wraps up the conflict.
questions.tip: The resolution resolves things: the problem gets solved.

questions.q: Which is an example of a character versus nature conflict?
choices: A sailor fights to survive a storm at sea.
Two friends argue about a game.
A girl struggles with a hard choice.
A student competes against a rival.
questions.explain: The storm is a force of nature working against the character.
questions.tip: Ask who or what the enemy is: a storm is nature.

questions.q: Which sentence contains a dangling modifier?
choices: Walking to school, the rain soaked my shoes.
Walking to school, I got soaked by the rain.
The rain soaked my shoes as I walked to school.
questions.explain: The first sentence says the rain was walking to school. A modifier must clearly attach to the right word.
questions.tip: Ask who is doing the -ing: if it is the wrong noun, the modifier dangles.

questions.q: Which sentence has correct parallel structure?
choices: She likes hiking, swimming, and biking.
She likes hiking, swimming, and to bike.
She likes to hike, swimming, and biking.
questions.explain: Items in a series should share the same grammatical form, here all gerunds.
questions.tip: Parallel structure is like parallel lines: every item runs in the same form.

questions.q: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
choices: I have a test tomorrow; I need to study.
Because I have a test; I need to study.
questions.explain: A semicolon joins two independent clauses. Neither side can be a fragment.
questions.tip: A semicolon is a balanced seesaw: a full sentence must sit on each side.

questions.q: Which sentence uses a colon correctly?
choices: Bring three things: a pen, a notebook, and a calculator.
Bring: a pen, a notebook, and a calculator.
Bring three things a pen: a notebook, and a calculator.
questions.explain: A colon should follow a complete independent clause that introduces a list or explanation.
questions.tip: A colon is a drumroll: complete sentence first, then the reveal.

questions.q: What is a gerund?
choices: A verb form ending in -ing used as a noun
A verb form used as an adjective
questions.explain: In 'Swimming is fun,' swimming is a gerund acting as the subject.
questions.tip: Gerunds are -ing verbs dressed up as nouns: Swimming is fun.

questions.q: In 'She wants to win,' the phrase 'to win' is...
questions.explain: An infinitive is 'to' plus the base form of a verb.
questions.tip: To plus a verb is an infinitive: to be, to win, to go.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses the subjunctive mood?
choices: If I were you, I would apologize.
If I was you, I would apologize.
questions.explain: For hypothetical or contrary-to-fact conditions, formal English uses 'were' for all subjects.
questions.tip: 'If I were a rich man': wishes and what-ifs take were.

questions.q: In 'My brother, a talented chef, made dinner,' what is the appositive?
questions.explain: An appositive is a noun phrase that renames the noun beside it.
questions.tip: An appositive is a name tag pinned beside a noun.

questions.q: Which sentence avoids a comma splice?
choices: The movie ended, and we went home.
The movie ended, we went home.
The movie ended we went home.
questions.explain: Two independent clauses need a comma plus a coordinating conjunction, a semicolon, or a period.
questions.tip: A comma alone can't hold two sentences: add a FANBOYS word or use a semicolon.

questions.q: In 'The book that I borrowed is overdue,' the words 'that I borrowed' form a(n)...
questions.explain: The clause describes the noun 'book', so it acts as an adjective.
questions.tip: A clause that describes a noun is an adjective clause, often starting with who, which, or that.

questions.q: Ethos is an appeal to...
questions.explain: Ethos persuades by showing the speaker is trustworthy or qualified.
questions.tip: Ethos sounds like ethics: it is about trusting the speaker's character.

questions.q: Pathos is an appeal to...
questions.explain: Pathos persuades by stirring the audience's feelings.
questions.tip: Pathos is in sympathy and empathy: it is about feelings.

questions.q: Logos is an appeal to...
questions.explain: Logos persuades with reasons, facts, and statistics.
questions.tip: Logos sounds like logic.

questions.q: A speaker begins, 'As a doctor with 20 years of experience...' Which appeal is this?
questions.explain: Stating qualifications builds the speaker's credibility.
questions.tip: Credentials build credibility, and credibility is ethos.

questions.q: A rhetorical question is...
choices: a question asked for effect, not to get an answer
a question that has no correct answer
a question asked in a debate rebuttal
a question that ends an essay
questions.explain: Rhetorical questions make a point, like 'Who doesn't want to be happy?'
questions.tip: A rhetorical question answers itself.

questions.q: Repeating a word or phrase at the start of successive clauses is called...
questions.explain: Anaphora, as in 'We shall fight... we shall fight...', builds rhythm and emphasis.
questions.tip: Anaphora repeats at the start, like 'I have a dream' said again and again.

questions.q: Kairos refers to...
choices: the timeliness or opportune moment of an argument
questions.explain: Kairos is about saying the right thing at the right time.
questions.tip: Kairos is timing: strike while the iron is hot.

questions.q: In an argumentative essay, a counterargument is...
choices: an opposing view that the writer addresses
questions.explain: Addressing counterarguments and rebutting them makes an argument stronger.
questions.tip: Counter means against: the counterargument is the other side's punch.

questions.q: A thesis statement is...
choices: a sentence stating the essay's main claim
a quotation that opens the essay
questions.explain: The thesis tells readers the central argument the essay will support.
questions.tip: Your thesis is the GPS for the whole essay.

questions.q: Speaker, audience, purpose, and context together make up the...
questions.explain: Analyzing the rhetorical situation helps explain the choices a writer makes.
questions.tip: Think SOAPS: Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject.

questions.q: A fire station burns down. This is an example of...
questions.explain: Situational irony is when the outcome is the opposite of what you would expect.
questions.tip: Situational irony: the situation flips the opposite way you expect.

questions.q: When the audience knows something a character does not, it is called...
questions.explain: In Romeo and Juliet, the audience knows Juliet is not dead, but Romeo does not.
questions.tip: Dramatic irony: in the drama, the audience is in on the secret.

questions.q: An allusion is...
choices: a reference to a well-known person, place, event, or work
a long speech by one character
questions.explain: Calling someone 'a Romeo' is an allusion to Shakespeare's character.
questions.tip: An allusion alludes, or points, to something famous.

questions.q: A soliloquy is...
choices: a speech in which a character alone on stage speaks their thoughts aloud
questions.explain: Hamlet's 'To be, or not to be' is a famous soliloquy.
questions.tip: Solo plus loquy (speaking): a soliloquy is a solo speech.

questions.q: How many lines does a traditional sonnet have?
questions.explain: Shakespearean and Petrarchan sonnets both have 14 lines.
questions.tip: A sonnet is a fortnight of lines: 14.

questions.q: 'Jumbo shrimp' is an example of...
questions.explain: An oxymoron puts contradictory words together.
questions.tip: Oxymoron comes from Greek for 'sharp' plus 'dull', so the word itself is a contradiction!

questions.q: An object that represents a larger idea, like a dove for peace, is a...
questions.explain: A symbol stands for something beyond its literal meaning.
questions.tip: A symbol is a stand-in, like a heart for love.

questions.q: A line of iambic pentameter usually has how many syllables?
questions.explain: Pentameter means five feet, and each iamb has two syllables: 5 x 2 = 10.
questions.tip: Penta means five, like a pentagon: five da-DUMs make 10 syllables.

questions.q: The author's attitude toward the subject is called...
questions.explain: Tone is the author's attitude. Mood is the feeling the reader gets.
questions.tip: Tone is the author's tone of voice; mood is how Me, the reader, feels.

questions.q: Satire is...
choices: using humor, irony, or exaggeration to criticize
a true account of one's own life
a story with talking animals and a moral
questions.explain: Satire mocks people, institutions, or ideas to expose flaws. Those other options describe an elegy, an autobiography, and a fable.
questions.tip: Think of a comedy sketch that mocks something to make a serious point.

questions.q: Who wrote 'Romeo and Juliet'?
questions.explain: Shakespeare wrote the tragedy in the 1590s.
questions.tip: Shakespeare's star-crossed lovers lived in fair Verona.

questions.q: Who wrote 'Pride and Prejudice'?
questions.explain: Jane Austen published Pride and Prejudice in 1813.
questions.tip: Austen's perfect pair, Elizabeth and Darcy, need to drop their pride and their prejudice.

questions.q: Who wrote 'The Great Gatsby'?
questions.explain: Fitzgerald published The Great Gatsby in 1925.
questions.tip: Fitzgerald's Gatsby throws glittering Jazz Age parties.

questions.q: Who wrote 'To Kill a Mockingbird'?
questions.explain: Harper Lee's novel was published in 1960 and won the Pulitzer Prize.
questions.tip: Harper Lee gave us Atticus, Scout, and a mockingbird you should never harm.

questions.q: Who wrote the novel '1984'?
questions.explain: George Orwell published 1984 in 1949.
questions.tip: Orwell's 1984: Big Brother is watching you.

questions.q: Who wrote 'Adventures of Huckleberry Finn'?
questions.explain: Mark Twain was the pen name of Samuel Clemens.
questions.tip: Twain sent Huck down the Mississippi, the river where Twain once piloted steamboats.

questions.q: Who wrote 'Of Mice and Men'?
questions.explain: Steinbeck published Of Mice and Men in 1937.
questions.tip: Steinbeck's George and Lennie dream of a farm of their own.

questions.q: The ancient Greek epic 'The Odyssey' is traditionally credited to...
questions.explain: Homer is credited with both the Iliad and the Odyssey.
questions.tip: Homer's hero Odysseus spends ten years trying to get home: Homer, home.

questions.q: Who wrote 'Frankenstein'?
questions.explain: Mary Shelley published Frankenstein in 1818.
questions.tip: Mary Shelley started Frankenstein at 18 during a ghost-story contest.

questions.q: Who wrote the poem 'The Raven'?
questions.explain: Poe published The Raven in 1845.
questions.tip: Poe's raven only ever says 'Nevermore'.

questions.q: Who wrote 'The Scarlet Letter'?
questions.explain: Hawthorne published The Scarlet Letter in 1850.
questions.tip: Hawthorne's Hester Prynne wears a scarlet letter A.

questions.q: What does 'ubiquitous' mean?
questions.explain: Something ubiquitous seems to be present everywhere at once.
questions.tip: Ubiquitous sounds like 'you be quick to find it', because it is everywhere.

questions.q: What does 'ephemeral' mean?
questions.explain: Ephemeral things, like a soap bubble, are fleeting.
questions.tip: Mayflies live about a day, and their scientific order is Ephemeroptera.

questions.q: What does 'benevolent' mean?
questions.explain: Benevolent comes from Latin for wishing well.
questions.tip: Bene means good, like benefit: a benevolent person wishes you well.

questions.q: What does 'candid' mean?
questions.explain: A candid answer is open and straightforward.
questions.tip: A candid photo catches you being your real self.

questions.q: What does 'meticulous' mean?
questions.explain: A meticulous person pays close attention to every detail.
questions.tip: A meticulous person ticks every tiny box.

questions.q: What does 'pragmatic' mean?
questions.explain: A pragmatic approach focuses on what will actually work.
questions.tip: Pragmatic and practical both start with P-R-A.

questions.q: What does 'ambivalent' mean?
questions.explain: Ambivalent means torn between opposite feelings. Using both hands equally is ambidextrous.
questions.tip: Ambi means both: ambivalent feelings pull both ways.

questions.q: What does 'eloquent' mean?
choices: fluent and persuasive in speaking or writing
questions.explain: An eloquent speaker expresses ideas clearly and movingly.
questions.tip: Eloquent contains 'loqu', Latin for speak, like loquacious.

questions.q: What does 'obsolete' mean?
questions.explain: Obsolete things, like floppy disks, have been replaced.
questions.tip: Obsolete: absolutely out of date.

questions.q: What does 'scrutinize' mean?
questions.explain: To scrutinize is to inspect carefully and critically.
questions.tip: Scrutinize: screw up your eyes and inspect every detail.

questions.q: What does 'tenacious' mean?
questions.explain: A tenacious person does not give up easily.
questions.tip: Tenacious grips like tentacles that won't let go.

questions.q: What does MLA stand for?
questions.explain: MLA style is common in English and the humanities.
questions.tip: MLA: Modern Language, the style of English class.

questions.q: What does APA stand for?
questions.explain: APA style is common in psychology and the social sciences.
questions.tip: APA: the P is for Psychology.

questions.q: In MLA style, the list of sources at the end of a paper is titled...
questions.explain: MLA uses 'Works Cited'. APA uses 'References'.
questions.tip: MLA lists the Works you Cited.

questions.q: In APA style, the list of sources at the end of a paper is titled...
questions.explain: APA uses a 'References' page.
questions.tip: APA: References for Research.

questions.q: An MLA in-text citation usually includes...
choices: the author's last name and page number
the author's full name and publisher
questions.explain: For example: (Smith 42).
questions.tip: MLA cares about the page: (Smith 42), no comma, no year.

questions.q: An APA in-text citation usually includes...
choices: the author's last name and year of publication
questions.explain: For example: (Smith, 2020). Add a page number for direct quotes.
questions.tip: APA cares about when: Author, Year.

questions.q: Plagiarism is...
choices: presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own
quoting a source with a citation
paraphrasing a source with a citation
questions.explain: Plagiarism includes copying without credit, even accidentally.
questions.tip: If it is not your idea, give credit where credit is due.

questions.q: If you paraphrase a source in your own words, do you need to cite it?
questions.explain: The ideas still belong to the original author, so paraphrases need citations.
questions.tip: Your words, their idea: still cite it.

questions.q: Which is common knowledge that usually does not need a citation?
choices: A statistic from a recent survey
A line quoted from a novel
questions.explain: Widely known, easily verified facts usually need no citation. Specific data, quotes, and opinions do.
questions.tip: If most people know it and it is easy to check, you usually don't need a citation.

questions.q: How are entries in an MLA Works Cited list ordered?
choices: In the order they appear in the paper
questions.explain: Entries are alphabetized, usually by the author's last name.
questions.tip: A Works Cited list is alphabetical, like a dictionary.

questions.q: In the Toulmin model, the assumption that connects the evidence to the claim is the...
questions.explain: The warrant explains why the data supports the claim.
questions.tip: The warrant is the bridge from evidence to claim.

questions.q: In the Toulmin model, a qualifier...
choices: limits the strength of a claim, using words like 'usually'
questions.explain: Qualifiers like 'probably' or 'in most cases' keep a claim from overreaching.
questions.tip: Qualifiers qualify: usually, often, probably.

questions.q: Deductive reasoning moves...
choices: from general premises to a specific conclusion
from specific observations to a general conclusion
from the conclusion back to the evidence
questions.explain: All humans are mortal; Socrates is human; so Socrates is mortal.
questions.tip: Deduction drills down: general to specific.

questions.q: Inductive reasoning...
choices: draws a general conclusion from specific observations
questions.explain: Inductive conclusions are probable, not certain, and depend on the strength of the evidence.
questions.tip: Induction inches up: examples to a general rule.

questions.q: A categorical syllogism consists of...
questions.explain: A syllogism has a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion.
questions.tip: A syllogism is two steps up and one conclusion out.

questions.q: A deductive argument is valid when...
choices: the conclusion must be true if the premises are true
all of its premises are true
questions.explain: Validity is about logical form. An argument can be valid even with false premises.
questions.tip: Valid means the logic machine works, even if you feed it bad parts.

questions.q: A deductive argument is sound when...
choices: it is valid and all of its premises are true
questions.explain: Soundness requires both valid form and true premises.
questions.tip: Sound equals valid plus true: a working machine with good parts.

questions.q: Aristotle's three modes of persuasion are...
questions.explain: In his Rhetoric, Aristotle described appeals to character, emotion, and reason.
questions.tip: Ethos, pathos, logos: character, heart, and head.

questions.q: A Rogerian argument emphasizes...
questions.explain: Based on Carl Rogers's ideas, it seeks understanding and compromise.
questions.tip: Rogerian: 'Roger that, I hear you.'

questions.q: In argument, a concession is...
choices: acknowledging a valid point made by the other side
questions.explain: A concession admits a point while still maintaining the overall claim.
questions.tip: Concede the battle to win the war.

questions.q: Attacking the person making an argument instead of the argument itself is...
questions.explain: Ad hominem is Latin for 'to the person'.
questions.tip: Ad hominem aims at the man, not the argument.

questions.q: Misrepresenting an opponent's position to make it easier to attack is...
questions.explain: A straw man argues against a distorted version of the real claim.
questions.tip: A straw man is easy to knock down because it is fake.

questions.q: 'Everyone is buying this phone, so it must be the best.' This is...
questions.explain: Popularity alone does not prove something is true or best.
questions.tip: Bandwagon: hop on because everyone else did.

questions.q: 'Either you support this plan, or you want the city to fail.' This is...
questions.explain: It presents only two options when others exist.
questions.tip: A false dilemma pretends there are only two doors.

questions.q: 'If we allow phones in class, soon students will never learn anything.' This is...
questions.explain: It claims one step will inevitably lead to an extreme outcome without support.
questions.tip: Slippery slope: take one step and you slide all the way down.

questions.q: 'I wore my lucky socks and we won, so the socks caused the win.' This is...
questions.explain: It assumes that because one event followed another, the first caused the second.
questions.tip: Post hoc means 'after this', and after is not the same as because.

questions.q: 'I met two rude people from that city, so everyone there is rude.' This is...
questions.explain: It draws a broad conclusion from too small a sample.
questions.tip: A hasty generalization jumps to conclusions too fast.

questions.q: 'He is trustworthy because he is an honest person.' This is...
questions.explain: The conclusion is simply restated as the premise.
questions.tip: Circular reasoning chases its own tail.

questions.q: Introducing an irrelevant topic to divert attention from the issue is...
questions.explain: A red herring leads the discussion away from the real question.
questions.tip: A red herring is a smelly fish dragged across the trail to throw the hounds off.

questions.q: 'You say I shouldn't eat junk food, but you eat it too.' This is...
questions.explain: Tu quoque ('you too') dismisses a claim by pointing to the speaker's hypocrisy.
questions.tip: Tu quoque means 'you too', but two wrongs don't make a right.

questions.q: 'A famous actor says this medicine works, so it must.' This is...
questions.explain: The actor is not an expert on medicine, so the endorsement is not evidence.
questions.tip: Famous is not the same as expert.

questions.q: Romanticism emphasized...
questions.explain: Romantics reacted against Enlightenment rationalism and industrialization.
questions.tip: Romantics romanticize nature and feelings.

questions.q: Which poet was a key figure of English Romanticism?
questions.explain: Wordsworth and Coleridge's Lyrical Ballads (1798) helped launch the movement.
questions.tip: Wordsworth 'wandered lonely as a cloud' among the daffodils.

questions.q: Which writer is associated with American Transcendentalism?
questions.explain: Thoreau, author of Walden, and Ralph Waldo Emerson led the movement.
questions.tip: Thoreau went to the woods at Walden Pond to live deliberately.

questions.q: Realism in literature aimed to...
choices: depict everyday life and ordinary people accurately
questions.explain: Realists like William Dean Howells and Henry James portrayed life as it is.
questions.tip: Realism keeps it real.

questions.q: Literary Naturalism portrays characters as...
choices: shaped by heredity, environment, and forces beyond their control
questions.explain: Writers like Stephen Crane and Theodore Dreiser applied a deterministic view to fiction.
questions.tip: Naturalism: nature and nurture decide your fate.

questions.q: Gothic literature typically features...
choices: dark settings, mystery, and the supernatural
questions.explain: Examples include Frankenstein and Dracula.
questions.tip: Gothic: think gargoyles, crumbling castles, and ghosts.

questions.q: Which writer is closely associated with Modernism and stream of consciousness?
questions.explain: Woolf's Mrs Dalloway and To the Lighthouse experiment with inner consciousness.
questions.tip: Woolf's characters' thoughts flow like a stream.

questions.q: The 'Lost Generation' refers to writers who came of age during...
questions.explain: Gertrude Stein's phrase described writers like Hemingway and Fitzgerald.
questions.tip: The Lost Generation felt lost after the Great War.

questions.q: Which poet was a leading figure of the Harlem Renaissance?
questions.explain: The Harlem Renaissance flourished in the 1920s and 1930s.
questions.tip: Hughes was the heartbeat of Harlem.

questions.q: Which writer is associated with the Beat Generation?
questions.explain: Kerouac's On the Road (1957) is a defining Beat novel.
questions.tip: Kerouac's Beats hit the road.

questions.q: Which writer is most associated with magical realism?
questions.explain: One Hundred Years of Solitude blends the fantastic with the everyday.
questions.tip: Magical realism: García Márquez makes magic feel ordinary.

questions.q: What does 'obfuscate' mean?
questions.explain: Jargon is sometimes used to obfuscate a simple idea.
questions.tip: Obfuscate sounds like fog: it clouds things up.

questions.q: What does 'perfunctory' mean?
choices: done routinely with little care or interest
questions.explain: A perfunctory nod is given out of duty, not interest.
questions.tip: Perfunctory: it functions, but with zero heart.

questions.q: What is a 'sycophant'?
choices: a person who flatters powerful people to gain favor
questions.explain: Sycophants tell those in power what they want to hear.
questions.tip: A sycophant is a flattering suck-up.

questions.q: What does 'recalcitrant' mean?
questions.explain: A recalcitrant student resists authority or guidance.
questions.tip: Recalcitrant comes from Latin for kicking back with the heel, like a stubborn mule.

questions.q: What does 'laconic' mean?
questions.explain: The word comes from Laconia, home of the famously terse Spartans.
questions.tip: Laconic speakers lack words.

questions.q: What does 'pernicious' mean?
choices: harmful, especially in a gradual or subtle way
questions.explain: A pernicious influence does damage that may go unnoticed.
questions.tip: Pernicious sounds like poison, and it works slowly like one.

questions.q: What does 'equivocate' mean?
choices: to use vague language to avoid committing
questions.explain: A politician who equivocates avoids giving a clear answer.
questions.tip: Equivocate: equal voices on both sides, so you say nothing.

questions.q: What does 'magnanimous' mean?
choices: generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival
questions.explain: A magnanimous winner is gracious to the loser.
questions.tip: Magna plus animus: a big soul.

questions.q: What does 'esoteric' mean?
choices: understood by only a small group with special knowledge
questions.explain: Esoteric topics require specialized knowledge.
questions.tip: Esoteric comes from Greek for 'inner': only for the inner circle.

questions.q: What does 'juxtapose' mean?
choices: to place side by side for comparison or contrast
questions.explain: Writers juxtapose images or ideas to highlight differences.
questions.tip: Juxtapose: just pose them side by side.

questions.q: What does 'didactic' mean?
choices: intended to teach, often with a moral lesson
questions.explain: Fables are didactic: they exist to teach a lesson.
questions.tip: Didactic comes from Greek didaskein, 'to teach'.

questions.q: Which sentence is in the active voice?
choices: The meal was cooked by the chef.
questions.explain: In active voice, the subject performs the action.
questions.tip: Active voice: the actor acts first.

questions.q: Which sentence is in the passive voice?
choices: The window was broken by the ball.
questions.explain: Passive voice uses a form of 'be' plus a past participle, and the subject receives the action.
questions.tip: Zombie test: if 'by zombies' fits after the verb, it is passive.

questions.q: When is the passive voice an appropriate choice?
choices: When the doer is unknown or unimportant
Always, because it sounds more formal
questions.explain: Passive voice is grammatical; it is useful when the action matters more than the actor.
questions.tip: Passive works when the 'who' doesn't matter: Mistakes were made.

questions.q: Most concise revision: 'Due to the fact that it was raining, we stayed inside.'
choices: Because it was raining, we stayed inside.
Owing to the fact that it was raining, we stayed inside.
Due to the fact of the rain, we stayed inside.
questions.explain: 'Due to the fact that' can almost always be replaced with 'because'.
questions.tip: 'Because' says it in one word.

questions.q: Most concise revision: 'In my personal opinion, I think the plan will work.'
choices: I think the plan will work.
In my opinion, I think the plan will work.
It is my personal opinion that the plan will work.
questions.explain: 'In my personal opinion' and 'I think' say the same thing.
questions.tip: Say it once: 'I think' already means it is your opinion.

questions.q: Which phrase is redundant?
questions.explain: All history is in the past, so 'past' adds nothing.
questions.tip: 'Past history' is like saying 'wet water'.

questions.q: Which single verb replaces the wordy 'make a decision'?
questions.explain: Turning a nominalization back into a verb makes writing more direct.
questions.tip: Free the verb hiding inside the noun: decision becomes decide.

questions.q: Most concise revision: 'There are many students who want to join.'
choices: There are many students wanting to join.
There exist many students who want to join.
questions.explain: Removing the empty 'there are... who' construction puts the real subject first.
questions.tip: 'There are... who' is scaffolding: tear it down.

questions.q: 'At this point in time' can usually be replaced with...
questions.explain: One word does the work of five.
questions.tip: Five words, one meaning: now.

questions.q: Which sentence uses the strongest, most concise verb?
choices: She ran very quickly to the bus.
She made her way very fast to the bus.
questions.explain: A precise verb like 'sprinted' replaces a weak verb plus adverbs.
questions.tip: Pick a verb that paints a picture.

questions.q: ___ should I call about the leak?
questions.explain: It is the object of 'call' (I should call him), so formal English uses 'whom'. Tip: him = whom.
questions.tip: Him equals whom: both end in m.

questions.q: ___ is at the door?
questions.explain: It is the subject of 'is' (he is at the door), so use 'who'.
questions.tip: He equals who: 'He is at the door.'

questions.q: To ___ it may concern:
questions.explain: After a preposition like 'to', use the object form 'whom'.
questions.tip: Prepositions want the m: to whom, for whom, with whom.

questions.q: She is the candidate ___ we believe will win.
questions.explain: Ignore 'we believe': who will win. 'Who' is the subject of 'will win'.
questions.tip: Cross out 'we believe' and test: he will win, so who.

questions.q: Give the award to ___ deserves it most.
questions.explain: The pronoun is the subject of 'deserves', so use 'whoever', even after 'to'.
questions.tip: Look at the verb inside the clause: he deserves it, so whoever.

questions.q: This stays between you and ___.
questions.explain: 'Between' is a preposition, so it takes the object pronoun 'me'.
questions.tip: Between you and me, 'between you and I' is a classic slip.

questions.q: There are ___ people here than yesterday.
questions.explain: Use 'fewer' with things you can count individually, like people.
questions.tip: Fewer for things you can count; less for stuff you can't.

questions.q: I have ___ patience than I used to.
questions.explain: Use 'less' with uncountable quantities, like patience or water.
questions.tip: You can't count patience, so less.

questions.q: We had ___ than five dollars left.
questions.explain: Sums of money, time, and distance are treated as amounts, so 'less' is standard.
questions.tip: Money is an amount: less money, but fewer coins.

questions.q: The new policy will ___ everyone.
questions.explain: Affect is usually the verb (to influence).
questions.tip: Affect is the Action, Effect is the End result.

questions.q: The medicine had a strong ___.
questions.explain: Effect is usually the noun (a result).
questions.tip: Effect is the End result.

questions.q: The new manager wants to ___ real change.
questions.explain: As a verb, 'effect' means to bring about. To effect change is to cause it.
questions.tip: To effect change is to Execute it.

questions.q: I'm going to ___ down for a nap.
questions.explain: 'Lie' means to recline and takes no object. 'Lay' means to put something down.
questions.tip: People lie down; you lay an object down.

questions.q: Please ___ the book on the table.
questions.explain: You lay an object somewhere. The book is the object.
questions.tip: Lay means place: both have an a.

questions.q: Yesterday, I ___ down for an hour.
questions.explain: The past tense of 'lie' (recline) is 'lay'. 'Laid' is the past of 'lay', and 'lied' means told a falsehood.
questions.tip: Lie, lay, lain: yesterday I lay down.

questions.q: He has ___ the tiles in the bathroom.
questions.explain: 'Laid' is the past participle of 'lay' (to put). 'Lain' belongs to 'lie', and 'layed' is a misspelling.
questions.tip: Lay, laid, laid works like pay, paid, paid.

questions.q: Which abbreviation means 'for example'?
questions.explain: e.g. stands for Latin exempli gratia, 'for the sake of example'.
questions.tip: e.g. = example given.

questions.q: What does 'i.e.' mean?
questions.explain: i.e. stands for Latin id est, 'that is'. It restates or clarifies.
questions.tip: i.e. = in essence.

questions.q: I love citrus fruits, ___ oranges and lemons.
questions.explain: Oranges and lemons are examples, not the complete list of citrus fruits.
questions.tip: e.g. = example given: just some of the list.

questions.q: She visited the capital of France, ___ Paris.
questions.explain: Paris is the one specific thing meant, so 'i.e.' (that is) fits.
questions.tip: i.e. = in essence: exactly that one.

questions.q: The ___ bone is buried in the yard. (one dog)
questions.explain: For a singular noun, add apostrophe plus s.
questions.tip: One dog: dog plus apostrophe-s.

questions.q: What is the possessive of 'children'?
questions.explain: For a plural that does not end in s, add apostrophe plus s.
questions.tip: Children is already plural, so just add apostrophe-s.

questions.q: We're going to the ___ house. (the Smith family)
questions.explain: The family is plural (the Smiths), so add just an apostrophe after the s.
questions.tip: Make it plural first (Smiths), then add the apostrophe.

questions.q: Which is the correct plural of the last name Johnson?
questions.explain: Plurals never take an apostrophe. Use one only for possession.
questions.tip: Apostrophes show ownership, not crowds.

questions.q: The company changed ___ logo.
questions.explain: Possessive 'its' has no apostrophe, like his and hers.
questions.tip: It's means it is; its works like his.

questions.q: ___ been a long day.
questions.explain: It's is a contraction of 'it has' here.
questions.tip: Expand it to check: it has been.

questions.q: Which is the standard way to write the decade?
questions.explain: Major American style guides (AP, Chicago, MLA, APA) write decades without an apostrophe.
questions.tip: The 1990s are many years, not one year owning something.

questions.q: Which possessive form of 'James' is incorrect?
questions.explain: The name is James, so the apostrophe can't go inside it. Chicago prefers James's, and AP uses James'.
questions.tip: Never cut a name in half with an apostrophe.

questions.q: Which grocery sign is correct?
questions.explain: Simple plurals take no apostrophe. Adding one is called the grocer's apostrophe.
questions.tip: Apples don't own anything, so no apostrophe.

questions.q: Sam and Ana share one car. Which is correct?
questions.explain: For joint ownership, only the last name gets the apostrophe. 'Sam's and Ana's cars' would mean separate cars.
questions.tip: One car, one apostrophe.

questions.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
choices: I was tired, so I went to bed.
I was tired so, I went to bed.
I was, tired so I went to bed.
questions.explain: Put a comma before a coordinating conjunction that joins two independent clauses.
questions.tip: Comma plus FANBOYS is strong enough glue for two sentences.

questions.q: Which sentence is a comma splice?
choices: I love coffee, I drink it daily.
I love coffee, and I drink it daily.
I love coffee; I drink it daily.
questions.explain: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.
questions.tip: A comma is too weak to hold two sentences on its own: that's a splice.

questions.q: The Oxford (serial) comma is the comma...
choices: before the final 'and' or 'or' in a list of three or more
questions.explain: Chicago and MLA require it; AP style generally omits it.
questions.tip: Without it, 'I thank my parents, a superhero and a pirate' makes your parents sound pretty exciting.

questions.q: You have one mother. Which sentence is correct?
choices: My mother, who lives in Ohio, is visiting.
My mother who lives in Ohio, is visiting.
My mother, who lives in Ohio is visiting.
questions.explain: A nonessential clause is set off by a pair of commas.
questions.tip: Extra info gets a comma hug on both sides.

questions.q: To say that only the students who studied passed, which is correct?
questions.explain: An essential (restrictive) clause takes no commas. With commas, it implies all the students studied.
questions.tip: Essential info gets no commas: you need it to know which students.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly invites Grandma to dinner?
questions.explain: Use a comma before a name in direct address. Commas save lives.
questions.tip: Let's eat, Grandma. Commas save lives!

questions.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
choices: When the meeting ended, everyone left.
When the meeting ended everyone, left.
When, the meeting ended everyone left.
questions.explain: Put a comma after an introductory dependent clause.
questions.tip: Intro clause, then a comma pause.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly punctuates coordinate adjectives?
choices: It was a long, hot day.
It was a long hot, day.
It was a, long hot day.
questions.explain: If you could put 'and' between the adjectives (long and hot), separate them with a comma.
questions.tip: If 'and' fits between the adjectives, a comma fits too.

questions.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
choices: On July 4, 1776, the Declaration of Independence was adopted.
On July 4 1776, the Declaration of Independence was adopted.
On July, 4, 1776 the Declaration of Independence was adopted.
questions.explain: In American style, a comma goes after the day and also after the year when the sentence continues.
questions.tip: Year in the middle of a sentence? Wrap it in commas.

questions.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
choices: She moved to Austin, Texas, last year.
She moved to Austin Texas, last year.
She moved to Austin, Texas last year.
questions.explain: Set off the state with commas on both sides when the sentence continues.
questions.tip: The state gets a comma before and after it.

questions.q: Should a comma separate a subject from its verb, as in 'The man in the blue coat, called me'?
questions.explain: Never put a single comma between a subject and its verb, even when the subject is long.
questions.tip: Never split a subject from its verb with a single comma.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct (meaning 'without doubt')?
questions.explain: Think of 'finite': de-FINITE-ly.
questions.tip: Definitely is definite plus ly: there is no a in sight.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct (meaning 'apart')?
questions.explain: There is 'a rat' in sep-a-rate.
questions.tip: There's a rat in separate.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct (meaning 'required')?
questions.explain: One c, two s's: like a shirt with one collar and two sleeves.
questions.tip: One collar, two sleeves: one c, two s's.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct (meaning 'to make room for')?
questions.explain: It is big enough to accommodate two c's and two m's.
questions.tip: Accommodate has room for two c's and two m's.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct (meaning 'an event')?
questions.explain: Double c, double r, and -ence: occurrence.
questions.tip: Occurrence: double c, double r, because things keep happening twice!

questions.q: Which spelling is correct (meaning 'to get')?
questions.explain: I before e, except after c: receive.
questions.tip: I before e, except after c.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct (meaning 'to make someone feel awkward')?
questions.explain: Embarrass has double r and double s.
questions.tip: Embarrass: you turn really red, so so shy: two r's, two s's.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct (meaning 'a thousand years')?
questions.explain: Double l and double n: from Latin mille (thousand) and annus (year).
questions.tip: A millennium is lots of years, so it gets lots of letters: two l's, two n's.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct (meaning 'a special right')?
questions.explain: There is no d in privilege.
questions.tip: Privilege alternates its vowels i, i, e, e, and has no d.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct (meaning 'a regular beat')?
questions.explain: Rhythm Helps Your Two Hips Move.
questions.tip: Rhythm Helps Your Two Hips Move.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct (meaning 'a go-between')?
questions.explain: Liaison has an i on both sides of the a: l-i-a-i-s-o-n.
questions.tip: Liaison has an i on each side of the a, like the two people it connects.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct (meaning 'a written survey')?
questions.explain: Questionnaire has double n and ends in -aire.
questions.tip: So many questions need two n's: questionnaire.

questions.q: Which spelling is correct (meaning 'now and then')?
questions.explain: Two c's, one s, two l's: occasionally.
questions.tip: Occasionally: two c's, one s, two l's.

questions.q: In traditional usage, 'nonplussed' means...
choices: confused and unsure how to react
questions.explain: Nonplussed traditionally means bewildered. Using it to mean 'unfazed' is a newer, informal sense many readers consider an error.
questions.tip: Nonplussed: no plus, no idea what to add or say.

questions.q: In careful usage, 'disinterested' means...
questions.explain: A disinterested judge is fair. Someone bored is 'uninterested'.
questions.tip: A DISinterested judge has no stake; an UNinterested listener is just bored.

questions.q: What does 'penultimate' mean?
questions.explain: Penultimate means next to last. It does not mean ultimate or supreme.
questions.tip: Pen means almost, as in peninsula (almost an island): penultimate is almost last.

questions.q: What does 'sanguine' mean?
questions.explain: A sanguine outlook is cheerful and hopeful.
questions.tip: Sanguine and sunny both start with S.

questions.q: What does 'pedantic' mean?
choices: overly concerned with minor rules and details
questions.explain: A pedantic person corrects small points to show off learning.
questions.tip: A pedant is a pain about tiny details.

questions.q: What does 'ameliorate' mean?
questions.explain: New policies may ameliorate a bad situation.
questions.tip: Ameliorate: like a good meal that makes you feel better.

questions.q: What does 'erudite' mean?
questions.explain: An erudite professor is deeply learned.
questions.tip: Erudite looks like 'e-rude', but erudite people are learned, not rude.

questions.q: What does 'hubris' mean?
questions.explain: In Greek tragedy, hubris often leads to a hero's downfall.
questions.tip: Hubris is the pride before the fall, like Icarus flying too close to the sun.

questions.q: What does 'cogent' mean?
questions.explain: A cogent argument is persuasive because its reasoning is sound.
questions.tip: A cogent argument fits together like well-oiled cogs.

questions.q: What does 'verbose' mean?
questions.explain: Verbose writing could say the same thing in fewer words.
questions.tip: Verbose writing is overloaded with words.

questions.q: In logic, 'begging the question' means...
choices: assuming the conclusion in the premise
questions.explain: It is circular reasoning. Using it to mean 'raises the question' is common but not the original sense.
questions.tip: Begging the question: the argument begs you to grant its own conclusion.
